definition: Certain to happen and impossible to avoid or prevent.
example: Once cracks began spreading across the old dam, costly repairs became inevitable.
nuance: Inevitable means nothing can stop an outcome, while likely or probable allows that it might still be avoided.
prompt: Campers watch the sun set on a clear, cold autumn evening in the mountains.
options: With the sun gone and the sky clear, a frosty night was inevitable.
Frost was inevitable, though the forecast said it would almost surely stay away.
Her inevitable campfire songs were so original that no one could ever copy them.
The inevitable flashlight turned out to be the most useful thing in his pack.
reasons: Clear autumn skies after sunset make a cold night certain; nothing the campers do can stop it.
An outcome that will almost surely not happen is the reverse of an unavoidable one.
Being impossible to copy describes inimitable, a look-alike, not something bound to occur.
Great usefulness suggests invaluable; a tool is not an event that must happen.

practice.prompt: A town library has kept the same aging computers for fifteen years.
options: Since the old machines break down every week, replacing them is inevitable.
Upgrading was inevitable, so the board easily decided never to do it at all.
The librarian made an inevitable choice by picking new models at random from a catalog.
The inevitable screens always showed the same gray menu and never changed.
reasons: When failures keep piling up, replacement will come sooner or later no matter what.
If the board can refuse forever, the upgrade was avoidable rather than certain.
A random pick is arbitrary, the opposite of something that had to turn out one way.
Never changing describes invariable; this word concerns outcomes that cannot be escaped.
